content:
Special Master Jose Linares has rejected the Department of Justice's (DOJ) request for review regarding allowing Apple to subpoena documents from 14 government agencies in the antitrust case. Details below.

Some background

In the DOJ's antitrust lawsuit against Apple, one of Apple's defense strategies involves the US government's own use of its products.

Apple's basic argument is that some of the practices challenged by the DOJ are actually reasonable security and privacy safeguards. To support this defense, Apple wants to know how federal agencies evaluate security and privacy when formulating smartphone policies and making procurement decisions.

To that end, Apple has been trying to obtain documents from the following 14 agencies:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

After Apple initially sought to force these agencies to turn over documents, the DOJ objected. The dispute was then referred to Special Master Jose Linares for a ruling.

Last month, Linares granted Apple's request, prompting the DOJ to file a motion for review. The DOJ argued that he applied the wrong legal standard, that Apple's request was unduly burdensome and disproportionate, and that the information sought was of limited relevance to the case.

Apple subsequently filed an opposition, calling the DOJ's motion "without merit at every level" and refuting the DOJ's arguments point by point.

Linares has now issued a new ruling, finding that none of the DOJ's arguments in support of its review request were persuasive, and maintaining the original ruling.

Apple gets the documents

The new ruling states:

The ruling also said that Linares believed "there is no reason to change course at this stage, whether or not it is persuasive," and added that "in this case, federal agencies are part of the United States with respect to document discovery by parties to the litigation."

The ruling states:

Plaintiff tries to make a mountain out of a molehill, arguing that under Rule 45 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, "non-parties to litigation enjoy a greater degree of protection from discovery than parties." [...] Therefore, Plaintiff argues that the inferences on which the Special Master's order and opinion are based are flawed because they do not cite or incorporate a Rule 45 analysis. The Special Master is familiar with Rule 45 and the different standards applicable to third-party discovery. A cursory review of the Special Master's opinion and order shows that Plaintiff's argument is incorrect. In fact, the Special Master has laid out in detail the genesis of this dispute. [...] A review of that portion of the opinion and order shows that the Defendant's need to issue a subpoena was itself caused by the Plaintiff.

The documents further explain that Linares considered these 14 federal agencies to be part of the United States, rather than third parties generally entitled to additional protections under Rule 45:

The documents also point out that the DOJ "misunderstands the legal framework applicable to the dispute in this case," and criticize the DOJ's claim that the information sought is of only "slight" relevance as "wholly unsupported by citation."

As a result, Apple is again permitted to subpoena documents from these 14 federal agencies.
